The post Follow the demand or preserve the breadth? Universities face an A-level dilemma appeared first on HEPI.
full_text:
This blog was kindly authored by Professor Alan Smithers, Centre for Education and Employment Research at the University of Buckingham

A-levels have served universities well over the years. At first, they were school qualifications and their main benefit to universities was identifying those who merited scholarships or bursaries to help with living costs before there were automatic grants. But gradually the universities ceded their exams to A-levels, and the relationship has become so close as to be symbiotic. As the university system expanded, the percentage of top grades rose from 10 per cent in 1965 to three times that in 2010. A-level entries also boomed from three to eight hundred thousand. There has always been a ready supply of respectably qualified applicants. But recently, with the reduced numbers from overseas, there is now an over-supply of places.

I am sure that university admissions tutors are well versed in what is happening to A-level entries and grades in their own subjects, but given that a university’s survival is dependent on applications, it is well worth taking a close look at what is happening across the piece. It is striking how students’ preferences are changing.

Maths has become much more popular, while English has fallen sharply. Twenty-five years ago, English had 87 thousand entrants to Maths’ 56 thousand, but last year while, Maths had grown to 112 thousand, English had fallen to just 58 thousand. French and German have also dropped spectacularly – declining by two-thirds and four-fifths since 1995 respectively. Spanish has bucked the trend, but has only reached an intake of eleven thousand.

In contrast, Psychology entries have quadrupled to 80 thousand, and Sociology has doubled to 40 thousand, although they have, particularly Sociology, waned somewhat recently. The Sciences have recovered well from the determined attempt on the creation of GCSEs to replace the separate subjects in Key Stage 4 with Combined Science. Physics entries, for example, fell from about 50 thousand in 1986 to 30 thousand in 2004, as the ladder was pulled away from under it. They survived thanks to the unlikely combination of independent schools, who fought the switch and won, and Gordon Brown, who, as Chancellor of the Exchequer, made them part of his 2004 Science Investment Strategy. The ground was laid for recovery and by 2025 A-level entries were back above 40 thousand.

Another challenge A-levels pose for universities is that different groups consistently differ in their results. Do universities seek to balance their intakes by adjusting entrance requirements or do they admit on merit and have uneven intakes?

The best example in the A-level results that are available through the Joint Council for Qualifications is the sex difference, though the reasoning will apply to ethnicity, social background, disability and neurodiversity. Girls outperform boys at every passing grade except A*. Boys are ahead here because they are much more likely to take and do well in high top-grade awarding quantitative subjects, such as Maths, the Physical Sciences and Economics.

Admitting on merit would lead imbalances in recruitment, with girls taking most of the places in the Arts, Humanities, and Social Sciences, while boys would cluster in the quantitative. This would apply not only to the subjects themselves, but to the professional courses that have particular subject requirements, such as Medicine and Engineering.

Adjusting entry requirements to balance the sexes has a long history. Girls did much better in the 11+, so boys had a lower pass threshold. It used to be the practice in Medicine, and perhaps still is, to limit the number of places available to girls. While invariably more presented with better qualifications, it was recognised that the purpose of the expensive training was to secure the future of the health service. When it was found that women were less likely to stay active in the profession, there was some rebalancing of the intake.

The dilemma is whether to give underperformers a leg up and be unfair to those who would be denied places or commit to pursuing excellence and accepting the imbalances. The decision is complicated by the requirements of the Office for Students, which has the power to take away university status.

The shifts in entries pose an even greater dilemma for universities. Do they focus on the bottom line and close departments where recruitment is evidently going to be difficult, such as English Literature, Modern Languages and the Arts in general, or do they contrive to keep them open to maintain intellectual breadth.

At first sight, it appears to be a no-brainer, without balancing the books, there will soon be no university – unless it has the necessary financial strength to survive through its assets and the generosity of donors. But people do not just go to university for a qualification; there is also the quality of the experience.

The logic of the bottom line is that a university will end up as a collection of silos of professional courses, like Medicine, Computing, Law and Business, each of which may in time decide that the rest of the university is an embarrassment and take off to set up independently.

The alternative is to maintain the breadth and keep a supportive environment in which students feel comfortable in pursuing their learning and staff in advancing the frontiers of their subjects. A mix of subjects with their own ‘truths’ provides a necessary check on reality, which is absorbed as the students and staff go about the campus. Left to their own devices subjects can go off in directions that are of little use and can be downright misleading.

Those are the two main issues I can see arising from the recent A-level results: What is to be done in response to the shifts in subject choices, and how are the consistently different levels of achievement between the various groups to be accommodated?

Failure to balance the books will lead to merger or bankruptcy; failure to provide a fulfilling university experience will lead to falling applications as the word gets round. Unless a university has strong and imaginative leadership to pilot a way through it, it will be either a rapid death or a slow death. It is Hobson’s choice!

title: UC Berkeley professor admits to using AI to edit op-ed on students’ math skills

A math professor at the University of California, Berkeley, criticizing a “severe” math deficiency among students in an op-ed for the San Francisco Standard, admitted to using artificial intelligence to help edit the piece.

full_text:
A math professor at the University of California, Berkeley, criticizing a “severe” math deficiency among students in an op-ed for the San Francisco Standard, admitted to using artificial intelligence to help edit the piece.

The Standard published a 2,000-word piece by Zvezdelina Stankova last week, in which the professor said some of her math students were “five to eight years” behind and lacked a “middle school” education on fractions and basic algebra. Stankova said the UC system’s test-blind admissions were to blame, suggesting that students who weren’t sufficiently prepared for the rigor of Berkeley’s mathematics program were admitted because a longstanding benchmark like the SAT had disappeared.

Over the weekend, journalists at Berkeley’s student newspaper, the Daily Californian, noticed the op-ed’s language sounded like AI. According to Berkeley sophomore Francis Luo, they ran it through AI-detection software Pangram, which claimed 33% of the op-ed had been generated or assisted by AI.

In response, Stankova admitted she had used AI software to “help edit the piece” but that the article was “the result of several hundred person-hours of intensive human work, of which about 80 hours are my own”.

Stankova said by email she had used AI to locate “numerous documents and articles related to the initiative” but that “all analysis is the result of the team members”.

When asked about their AI usage policy, the Standard – which published the op-ed – shared this statement by email: “While AI may assist, our expectation is that humans are behind every article we publish and take responsibility for every word. Our understanding in working with the author of this op ed was – and continues to be – that this piece reflects her and her colleagues’ extensive original analysis, research and expertise.”

Stankova’s admission has prompted a larger debate on social media on the use of AI by academics. Some criticized Stankova, calling its use “ironic” for a piece discussing students’ underpreparedness, or arguing an op-ed should have been entirely original and written without artificial assistance. Others defended the professor, saying the use of AI was not a serious issue and distracted from the argument at hand.

Stankova, in her email, said “the issue of how AI was used … is orthogonal to and a distraction from the thousands of hours our team has put into the initiative” of reinstating standardized tests in admission.

The debate over whether tests like the SAT or ACT should be again used in UC admissions has intensified over recent years. In 2020, the UC regents voted to phase out the tests as a requirement for application; so did institutions like Harvard, Stanford, MIT and Yale. Each of those peer colleges have since reinstated the requirement.

In her op-ed, Stankova shared data that she and her peers had analyzed, which suggested that the number of students with a “severe deficit” in their readiness for a calculus I class had tripled after test-blind admissions were introduced. Prior to publishing her op-ed last week, Stankova – in addition to more than 3,000 other UC faculty members – signed a June letter supporting admissions testing. Stankova, one of the letter’s authors, said AI was also used for editing there.

The UC academic senate said in a late July statement that it would begin a review to determine whether standardized tests would again be used in admissions. If reinstated, the changes would affect fall 2028 admissions at earliest.

The UC system also has its own “AI council”, which helps develop AI initiatives and resources for its colleges. Camille Crittenden, a member of the council, said she was unaware whether faculty had any specific guidance regarding the use of AI in personal research or editorials, but said that “most AI detection tools are still quite unreliable and lack nuance” with regard to Pangram.

On its website, Pangram claims it correctly identifies AI-generated documents 99.66% of the time, or gives one false positive about every 24,000 documents scanned.

title: ‘It’s easy to slip into the negatives’: students on their biggest financial shocks at university
summary:
From bank accounts to rent and food, students and recent graduates offer advice to those beginning to study

  • Student bank accounts: don’t be swayed by freebies

  • The best student deals and discounts

  • An insider’s tips on student money

We asked students, and recent graduates, to tell us about the biggest financial shock they had when they started university, and what advice they had for freshers.

Continue reading...
full_text:
We asked students, and recent graduates, to tell us about the biggest financial shock they had when they started university, and what advice they had for freshers.

George Gribben, third year, University of Brighton

Biggest shock

The price of public transport is ridiculous. I pay the same price back home in Switzerland, but the trains and buses are actually on time – I want to visit my best friend, who goes to university in Exeter, but it’s £90 to get there.

Advice

Get into cycling: buying a secondhand bike is cheaper in the long run than all of the bus and train tickets. And try to befriend people who have cars.

Elodie Clements, master’s, LSE

Biggest shock

Moving to London from a rural part of West Yorkshire I knew it was very expensive, but I didn’t realise just how big the margin between spending at home, versus at university, would be until I was doing my weekly shop and getting the tube.

Advice

Track your spending weekly as well as monthly. It’s easiest to do this by opening another bank account on top of whatever your student account is, and transferring a weekly allowance into it. I used Monzo. If I had any money left over from the week before, I’d transfer it into my savings account – giving me a bit extra at the end of term if I ran out of money, that could gain interest in the meantime.

Charlotte Farrow, third year, University of Brighton

Biggest shock

The rent in the second year. I lived in cheaper halls in the first year and left sorting my second-year accommodation to the last minute. The quality of my house was poor – mould, leaks and a faulty washing machine. It was £700 a month, without bills. It definitely gave me a reality check.

Advice

There’s no harm in being proactive: you’ll know people looking for houses as early as the November before. But from experience you can still find good deals later on. Just ensure you know who you want to live with first – and check for mould.

Jess Mallaghan, 2026 graduate, Loughborough University

Biggest shock

How many people received an allowance, or financial support, from their parents. I went to university in the Midlands, so the cost of living was not too bad, but a lot of the more sheltered students really struggled as they had never had to budget or cook before.

Advice

Split your student finance by month. Allocate a certain amount every month. If you can, have a small reserve. You will need more in the first month or two. I made the mistake of not worrying about money during freshers’ week and, by January, I was struggling.

Mathonwy Akuwimi, third year, University of Leicester

Biggest shock

The day-to-day cost of maintaining a healthy balanced diet. I realised how expensive everyday essentials were becoming, and how costly it can be just to simply eat well.

Advice

Budget carefully from the start, and shop at places such as Aldi or Lidl to help keep costs under control.

Farryn Stock, graduate, University for the Creative Arts

Biggest shock

The equipment and software they expected everyone to pay for. Before the course, they told us we would need Adobe software downloaded. They also suggested we got an Apple Mac as it was easier to use for creative courses. I hadn’t even written my first article before forking out a grand.

Advice

Something that really helped me was a NatWest student account. They offer an interest-free overdraft, perfect if you’re ever in a tight spot one month.

Charlotte Smith, 2026 graduate, University of Sheffield

Biggest shock

Early on in my degree, I opened an overdraft as a safety net for the financial struggles I had encountered. I was shocked at how easy and common it is to slip into the negatives. It got to a point where I used to avoid checking my balance because I feared how close I was to maxxing my funds out.

Advice

Invest some time in creating a budget tracker that works for you – and refrain from offering to buy a round with money that you may need to pay the bills.

title: The dangers of politicians being 'too online' - or not online enough
summary: In an era when reputations can be made or broken with a single post, getting the balance right is tricky.
full_text:
In early 2015, flower crowns started appearing on Ed Miliband's head. Petals and hearts were photoshopped on to the then-Labour leader by the "Milifandom", a movement of young, mostly female, voters sharing romanticised images on Twitter to protest against Miliband's "distorted media portrayal".

It was the brainchild of Abby Tomlinson, a 17-year-old sixth-form student, who came to the defence of the man she called "Milibae". The hashtag #Milifandom trended. Then Labour lost the 2015 election.

This prompted David Cameron, whose Conservatives increased their number of seats, to boast: "Britain and Twitter are not the same thing." Tomlinson later told me that having her hopes of Milibae in No10 dashed had made her a "political pessimist", after realising winning over voters online "doesn't happen in a day, a week or even months, it's going to take years".

More than a decade on and she is again using social media to big up a Labour leader, but this time in the heart of government. She sits in the press office in No 12 Downing Street as head of content for Andy Burnham. The government has spent the last few weeks recruiting producers, videographers and strategists, working out of both Whitehall and No 10 North in Manchester.

In his first month as PM, Burnham posted more than 50 times on Instagram, ranging from meetings with world leaders, campaigners, farmers and influencers, to meme-based content like ranking pub snacks with Chancellor John Healey as part of an announcement on business rates. Strategists believe Instagram and TikTok can play to Burnham's communication strengths and sense of humour.

They're all at it, of course. Videos of Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch tearing into the budget or mocking ex-PM Sir Keir Starmer have gone viral. Reform UK's Nigel Farage has by far the biggest online audience of any UK party leader, with 7.6 million followers across Facebook, Instagram, X, TikTok and YouTube.

In Scotland, the SNP have long mobilised their online army to campaign for independence, building a following larger than that of the Lib Dems, which campaigns across Britain, whose leader Ed Davey has achieved some success with campaign stunts going viral.

Restore Britain, founded by former Reform MP Rupert Lowe, enjoys its highest level of support among users of X. The platform is owned by Elon Musk who has publicly endorsed the party, expanding its reach.

Plaid Cymru, newly installed in government in Wales, is still experimenting with its approach, using First Minister Rhun Ap Iorweth in "fun" memes while also posting more serious interview excerpts. The Greens' Zack Polanski has made much of running his own accounts, though as he has found in recent weeks, this comes with risks too.

So how much is enough? In a world where reputations can be made (or broken) with one comment or collaboration, getting the balance right is tricky – being accessible, authentic and approachable, without being cringe. And does it make any difference to elections?

Cameron's successor, Theresa May, was similarly doubtful about the merits of social media. When she took office she rebuffed aides who suggested she start tweeting: "People don't say 'pass me the hashtag newspaper, or I'd like a hashtag coffee'." Announcements were to be made formally. When cabinet ministers were appointed in May's first reshuffle, it was heralded in press statements beneath the UK government coat of arms.

By contrast, this summer, presenting my 5 Live show from Downing Street during Burnham's first reshuffle, I could predict the appearance of another new minister because the two-person social media team from No 10 would move into position to capture the new arrivals on their cameras.

Of course, prime ministers (and wannabes) have long adapted to new technology. Winston Churchill harnessed the power of radio, but thought television a vulgar diversion. In the 1960s, Labour's Harold Wilson modelled his TV campaigning on JFK in America. In the 1990s, and 2000s leaders like Tony Blair were just as likely to be found on the chatshow sofa as on the Today programme.

Now, podcasts give long-form - and less combative - opportunities to connect with voters, while social media gives a quick hit of direct democratic dopamine.

Peter Hyman, a former adviser to both Tony Blair and Keir Starmer when in Downing Street, said the success of Burnham's early digital output was about "quantity as well as quality".

"You have to narrate the story of what you are doing three or four or five times a day so that you are out there regularly," Hyman said. "Keir Starmer wasn't out there enough and therefore it wasn't landing."

There is a causality dilemma here. Is Burnham more popular in the polls because he is racking up the likes on social media, or is he doing better online because people like him?

Not everyone is convinced. Cody Dahler, a comedian who posts sweary political explainers to his two million followers, warns voters will become cynical if they sense politicians are just using social media simply "as a comms tool". Burnham, Dahler told me on Newsnight, comes across like a "cool substitute teacher".

And after Burnham released a video discussing what a bread roll is called in different parts of the country – barm, cob or bap - to promote his plans for devolution, broadcaster Piers Morgan asked him to "stop wasting your time and ours with these cringe videos".

And therein lies the difficulty of striking a balance. Bea Timpson, a former press secretary to Liz Truss and Rishi Sunak who says she prefers "trad media" like broadcast and print, added: "I have to accept that it's now non-negotiable to be online a bit, but you definitely can be too much."

TV and online websites remain the most used sources for news, but more and more of us say we also get news from social media, according to media watchdog Ofcom. While this is highest among 16-24 year olds at 78%, a majority of adults in every age group use social media to access news, apart from the over-65s. Even among over 75s, 22% find out what is happening in the world from social media. For politicians, this is no longer just about reaching young people – this is all voters.

Some platforms are more important than others. Even after Elon Musk's conversion of Twitter into X, you will still see MPs, spin doctors and journalists in the Westminster village scrolling through the platform, but digital strategists say "real voters" are found on other platforms. The main parties have far more followers on Facebook (four million combined), which is much more widely used overall, than X (where they have a combined 3.2 million).

Politicians have always looked abroad for policy and campaigning ideas, and social media is no different.

Those on the right seek to emulate the impact Donald Trump has on TruthSocial, while left-wing politicians look to the success of Zohran Mamdani becoming mayor of New York.

Some have even imported social media experts from overseas. In 2019 Boris Johnson hired New Zealand duo Ben Guerin and Sean Topham to run the digital campaign for the general election. They imported into UK politics the concept of "shitposting", releasing deliberately bad images in order to generate a reaction. This included posting a tweet featuring the slogan "Get Brexit Done" in Comic Sans, a font loathed by graphic designers.

There was a method in the madness. "People are more likely to engage with something if they feel like it's been written by a human, not by a committee of design experts," Guerin told me. "It's pretty easy to go viral for doing something weird and wacky, but that doesn't always advance the objectives of your campaign."

This seems to be borne out by some recent hits. Burnham's TikTok post rating pub snacks attracted a million views. Yet a less gimmicky video, straightforwardly listing the five things he said he had done in his first week as PM, got five million.

There is an inherent tension in political social media. Authenticity is key. Yet who really expects the prime minister to be shooting and uploading his own content?

Back in 2013 I wrote a story about how Cameron's Twitter account had favourited a tweet mocking William Hague from an account handle that made a crude joke about former Tory MP Norman Tebbit being injured in the Brighton bombing.

The prime minister's director of communications called me to complain about my "slapdash and crappy" reporting. My crime? Including a sentence which allowed for the possibility that someone other than Cameron had clicked on the like button by mistake. This would, apparently, spoil the magic for those that thought the prime minister was running his own account for his 500,000 followers.

We now know that Zack Polanski does indeed have his own log-ins. The leader of the Green Party in England and Wales faced criticism in May for sharing a post condemning police actions in the Golders Green attack, for which he apologised. Then in July he accepted an Instagram collaboration which included a man wearing a T-shirt featuring a cartoon guillotine and the song lyrics "we're only making plans for Nigel". Reform UK said it amounted to incitement of violence against Farage. "I'm accepting my responsibility in that I shouldn't have accepted that collaboration," Polanski said, but refused to apologise.

Reform UK's Gawain Towler, a long-time media adviser to Nigel Farage, says: " My big takeaway is: don't be a berk on social media, which I think was Zack Polanski's big takeaway too."

And this in turn raises the question of how long the Burnham digital honeymoon might last. Can a prime minister TikTok his way through a war, terror attack or controversial court case? Announcing a new giveaway may go viral, but what about the details of the cuts to pay for it?

The truth is none of this is new, as Hyman explains: "The politicians who get this wrong think that social media is now the only place to be, and a substitute for doing the hard work and the heavy lifting of actually getting the right policy, getting the right narrative, and telling that story properly," he says. "Politics is about winning arguments."

After all, politicians have always wanted to be liked. It's just these days they can see it instantly if you hit that heart button on your feed.

Listen to Matt Chorley live from Westminster, weekdays from 14:00 on BBC Radio 5 Live.

title: The Financial Aid Community Needs Clarity and Accountability From ED
summary:
The Financial Aid Community Needs Clarity and Accountability From ED sara.custer@in… Wed, 08/19/2026 - 10:20 AM

And it needs more critical coverage of the sweeping regulatory changes administrators are being asked to implement.

Byline(s)
Letters to the Editor
full_text:
To the editor,

I am writing in response to the recent article, “ED Clarifies How Current Students Can Access Uncapped Loans” (Aug. 17, 2026).

In the article, a Department of Education spokesperson stated that using completed credits to calculate Expected Time to Credential (ETTC) under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act is “not new” and should “not come as a surprise.” As a financial aid administrator with more than 20 years of experience, I found that statement both astonishing and inconsistent with the guidance institutions have been given to date.

In the Department’s own May 2026 FAQ document, ETTC is described as “the expected time for a student to complete a program that is equal to the lesser of three academic years … or the period determined by calculating the difference between the program length for the program of study in which the individual is enrolled and the period of such program of study that such individual has completed prior to July 1, 2026.” Nowhere was it clearly communicated that institutions should determine ETTC using completed credits in the manner recently described by the department.

This latest clarification is not occurring in a vacuum. Since the enactment of OBBBA, the financial aid community has struggled through shifting interpretations, delayed guidance and significant uncertainty surrounding implementation. Colleges and universities have been asked to operationalize sweeping regulatory changes affecting students’ ability to borrow and finance their education, often without the clear and timely direction necessary to do so responsibly.

What makes this situation particularly troubling is the timing. Many institutions began awarding aid packages months ago. Schools have already notified students of their eligibility, finalized financial aid offers and in many cases disbursed funds. Revising a fundamental interpretation of eligibility requirements midway through August, after academic terms have already begun at some institutions, creates unnecessary disruption for students and administrative chaos for schools.

Financial aid professionals are not resisting change. We are asking for clarity, consistency and accountability. Our responsibility is to accurately implement federal policy on behalf of students. That task becomes nearly impossible when guidance evolves without acknowledgment of prior interpretations and institutions are told they should have anticipated changes that were never clearly communicated.

I was disappointed that the article did not more critically examine the discrepancy between the department’s prior guidance and its current position. Multiple voices quoted in the piece described a significant shift in interpretation, yet the department’s assertion that this approach was always understood went largely unchallenged.

The financial aid community deserves coverage that reflects the reality of what institutions have experienced throughout the implementation of OBBBA: uncertainty, moving targets and an ongoing struggle to obtain clear answers. Most importantly, students deserve better than policy changes and reinterpretations that occur after schools have already built their aid processes around the guidance provided.

title: 42% of Colleges Haven’t Fully Submitted Required Student Outcomes Data
summary:
42% of Colleges Haven’t Fully Submitted Required Student Outcomes Data
jessica.blake@… Wed, 08/19/2026 - 03:00 AM

The Education Department is giving the more than 1,900 colleges missing some or all Financial Value Transparency data one last chance. Noncompliance could bring consequences.

Byline(s)
Jessica Blake
full_text:
The Education Department’s Office of Federal Student Aid is warning hundreds of institutions that their access to federal grants and loans could be at risk if they fail to properly submit required student outcomes data by early 2027.

Newly released data shows that of more than 4,640 colleges and universities with programs eligible for funding, about 1,930 are either missing or have underreported some or all of the data they are required to provide under federal accountability rules.

That’s about 42 percent of the institutions in the database department officials attached to the warning. A deeper Inside Higher Ed analysis of the data shows that 578 of those institutions—or roughly 30 percent—haven’t properly submitted any of the seven required files, which span three academic years.

Out of the 1,930 institutions missing some data, the largest groups are for-profit colleges and those focused on certificate programs. But some notable public four-year institutions are on the list, too, including the University of Montana, the University of Central Oklahoma, Texas Southern University and at least 28 historically Black colleges and universities. (Inside Higher Ed reached out to five of the four-year institutions for comment but did not hear back by publication time.)

The missing data is raising concerns among student advocates and those who want to see institutions held accountable that ED won't have all the data it needs to most accurately measure whether college programs pass a new earnings test, which took effect July. ED says it has the data it needs, so it's concern is that the failure of colleges to fully submit the data represents a violation of federal law. The first round of data and test results is slated for release next year.

“Any new data collection comes with some amount of growing pains, and so it is normal to see some amount of initial noncompliance,” said Clare McCann, a former Biden staffer and now managing director of the Postsecondary Education and Economics Research Center at American University. But “completing mandatory data reporting is absolutely a requirement of schools’ agreements with the Department of Education [in order to receive federal aid]. So if schools are unwilling to complete the data collections that they are required to complete, the secretary can and should take action.”

The American Council on Education, one of the largest lobbying groups for higher education, said that it’s talking to its member institutions to “better understand the issue.” But it seems to have a lot to do with institution size, said ​​​Emmanual Guillory, ACE’s senior director of government relations.

“This could be a direct result of institutional capacity and potential confusion with changes in the reporting deadlines and requirements given the passage of the One Big Beautiful Bill for other institutions on the list,” Guillory explained.

Since July 1, 2024, colleges have been required to submit new program-level data on an annual basis, including information about whether the program meets licensure requirements and the total cost of attendance. Colleges also have to report a student’s total debt when they exit a program and the amount of private loans students received, among other items. (Only programs with more than 30 completers total over a four-year period are required to submit.)

That first batch of data was initially due July 31, 2024, and would include stats from 2022–23 and 2023–24. But the Education Department repeatedly pushed the deadline back until Sept. 30, 2025. Data from the 2024–25 academic year was due Oct. 1, 2025. In two months, on Oct. 1, 2026, institutions will have to submit data from 2025–26.

ED plans to use the data to compare the earnings of a program’s average graduate with those of a high school diploma holder in the same state. Programs that fail the test in two out of three consecutive years could temporarily lose access to federal loans.

The dataset from the Office of Federal Student Aid doesn’t specify what specific data points are missing. Rather, it lists the submission status for seven larger data files—one for 2022–23, and three each for 2023–24 and 2024–25.

McCann explained that the Office of Federal Student Aid has access to other data it can use to fill in the gaps. But if this trend continues and colleges still aren’t turning their data in after the first several rounds, then they could face larger consequences.

“I can’t speculate on what [punitive actions] the department plans to use, but they certainly have a lot of tools at their disposal, including [charging fines] against a school for failing to submit their required reporting,” she said. “I think colleges should have a strong interest in engaging in this process with the department to make sure that any information that is being produced under these rules is going to be as accurate as possible.”

Colleges with missing data have until Jan. 15, 2027, to comply with the reporting requirements. After that, department officials say, “incomplete or inaccurate submissions may raise concerns about an institution’s administrative capability to continue participating in the [federal student aid] programs.”

Breaking Down the Data

Michael Itzkowitz, who helped to develop the College Scorecard during the Obama administration, said it’s important to note the number of for-profit institutions that haven’t submitted some or all of their data. Roughly 1,400 for-profit institutions are listed in ED’s dataset, and 819 of them have at least one data file that wasn’t properly submitted—that’s nearly 60 percent.

By comparison, 526 public institutions are missing some data out of about 1,700 total—that’s about 30 percent.

“There’s more work to be done when it comes to getting a complete data file submitted and received through the department,” said Itzkowitz, who is now president of the HEA Group, a higher ed research organization. “Hopefully this notice will encourage institutions to re-evaluate their data and ensure that they’re submitting correct information to the right place.”

Inside Higher Ed’s analysis also shows that at least 415 of the 1,900 institutions missing some or all data are focused on cosmetology or massage therapy—many of which follow for-profit models. Department data has shown that cosmetology schools are predicted to have some of the highest fail rates of any type of institution under the earnings test.

Jordan Wicker, senior vice president of legislative and regulatory affairs at Career Education Colleges and Universities, a leading lobbying group for cosmetology schools and other for-profit institutions, said that CECU’s members represent “a small percentage” of the institutions with missing or underreported data.

“It can be challenging for institutions to determine exactly what information is missing because underreporting can encompass several different issues,” he said. “It is important to note that an institution’s inclusion on the list does not necessarily mean it intentionally failed to report or intentionally underreported its data.”

McCann from PEER also noted that the significant gap between colleges that are missing or have underreported just one file and those that haven’t turned in any may be a sign that some of the submission issues are rooted in confusion, as the deadlines and accountability rules have shifted over the last year.

“For a lot of institutions, I think they saw the Trump administration come in and begin to re-regulate on these issues and they took it as a pass on some of the reporting,” McCann said. The department’s recent announcement “is a good reminder to the schools of what they need to be doing. It offered some clarity.”

In addition to small for-profit institutions, McCann, Itzkowitz and others say the colleges most likely to struggle when submitting their data are the smaller institutions or those with low administrative capacity, many of which are private nonprofit colleges.

Out of the 578 institutions that are missing or underreported data files, 28 are HBCUs. That’s about a third of the 99 HBCUs recognized by ED. HBCUs have historically faced underfunding compared to other public and nonprofit four-year institutions, and the gap in resources could explain why so many appear on the department’s list.

“Compiling the necessary components for this reporting likely has and will continue to place an even more acute administrative burden on lower-resourced schools that were already stretched thin,” said Karen McCarthy, vice president of federal relations at the National Association of Student Financial Aid Administrators.

Public community and technical colleges also struggled to submit all the data, according to ED’s list. Although there were fewer community colleges on the list than for-profit institutions, they enrolled the largest number of undergraduate students.

Collectively, more than 492,600 undergraduate degree-seeking students attend an institution that hasn’t fully submitted any of the seven data files. Nearly 283,000 of them attend a public college that lists associate degrees or certificates as their predominant credential. All five of the top institutions that had missed or unreported all seven files when it came to enrollment were community colleges in Texas or California.

DeRionne Pollard, president of the American Association of Community Colleges, another higher ed lobbying group, said, “Community colleges are committed to complying with these requirements.”

She added that doing so will require close partnership with department staff “to ensure that all campuses have the support and guidance they need to provide these data records” and stressed that the department’s recent announcement only further reinforces the need for a better system to collect student outcomes data.

(2:10 p.m., Aug. 19: Updated to correct that the Education Department says it has the data necessary to run the earnings test.)

title: Students’ Choices of Roommates, Clubs and More Fuel Higher Ed Polarization
summary:
Students’ Choices of Roommates, Clubs and More Fuel Higher Ed Polarization
Ryan Quinn Wed, 08/19/2026 - 03:00 AM

A new book by sociologist Neil Gross argues universities aren’t doing enough to counteract students’ formation of their own ideological bubbles.

Byline(s)
Ryan Quinn
full_text:
Every day, conservatives accuse universities of being too liberal—indoctrinating students rather than teaching them. Neil Gross, a Colby College sociology professor who teaches a course called College in Crisis, has written a new book that argues polarization is a major problem on campuses. But he says students are largely fueling it, and colleges aren’t doing enough to counteract their ideological self-isolation.

Gross conducted nationally representative surveys of four-year undergraduates and interviewed 100 undergrads and recent alumni across 18 institutions, research that went into his new book, What Happened to College? How Politics Broke Higher Education and What We Can Do to Fix It (Simon & Schuster). His book describes how students form their own political bubbles through their selection of roommates, friends, lovers, clubs, majors and even the universities they attend.

Gross spoke with Inside Higher Ed via phone. This transcript has been edited for length and clarity.

Q: The title of your book is a question: What happened to college? Can you tell me what happened?

A: The answer is polarization.

Higher education has lots of problems and lots of good things going for it. Cost is one of those problems. Attacks from the federal government are another one. But the core problem I’m concerned with in this book is the effect of political polarization.

We’re very used to talking about the effects that polarization has had on other institutions, like the Supreme Court, Congress [and] the judiciary more generally.

Polarization has also upended much of the college experience.

It’s really changed the way that the undergraduate experience is organized, from where students choose to go to college to whom they become friends with, what they major in and what classes they take, and the argument is that’s not good. In particular, a form of polarization called affective polarization—which is when people with different beliefs come to not simply hold different views, but see the other side as evil—has crept into more and more of the college experience.

Q: Can you drill down a little bit more into what ways colleges and their students have become polarized?

A: Part of the issue is that the country as a whole has become polarized, and as that’s happened, it’s just filtered down into higher education. But I’ll give you a good example, which is in college admissions and the college search.

It’s always been the case that some very politically committed students have paid attention to the politics of their university and have maybe sought out schools with like-minded students. But the evidence suggests that is much more the case now than it was 20 or 30 years ago. A nontrivial number of students are very aware of the political reputation of their schools when they’re applying.

This is especially so for students applying to more selective schools, but it’s also true across the board. They’re interested not just in whether the school has a reputation for being liberal or conservative, but also in things like whether the school has a reputation for being political or not.

Students are still prioritizing things like cost and proximity and academic quality, but [politics is] there in the background for a lot of students. And one result is that we’re seeing a growth of some colleges that are becoming considerably more progressive in the leanings of the student body, [and] other colleges that are becoming more conservative in the leanings of the student body. So we’re getting almost two different sets of academic institutions.

Q: You write, “In 1982, some 20 percent of first-year students described themselves as liberal or far left. By 2019, that number had almost doubled, to 37 percent.” You also write that students who identified as middle-of-the-road declined significantly, while conservative/far-right–identifying students remained at about 20 percent. So, isn’t the increasing polarization of students before they get to college the real source of polarization here?

A: Those pre-existing attitudes of students before they come to campus is a big part of the story.

But there is additional polarization that takes place once students get to campus, and beyond that, there are ways in which campuses should be working to counter polarization that they’re not.

The particular kind of polarization that’s of interest to me, or of greatest concern to me, is this affective polarization, where people on one or the other side of the issue not only disagree with their ideological opponents, but really feel that the other side is immoral. [They] regard them with a great sense of dislike or even hatred, and that’s what higher education should be countering.

Students are coming into college with these already affectively polarized attitudes. When they get there, they end up sorting through the college experience in ways that keep them from talking to that many people with different views, and therefore not putting them in a position to really counter those stereotypes.

Q: Wouldn’t a better book title have been “What Happened to America”? Wouldn’t efforts to address polarization in college be fruitless, considering polarized society as a whole will just keep repolarizing colleges and the students once they graduate?

A: It could well be the case that the trend toward polarization that we’re seeing in the broader society can’t be countered by the actions of institutions. But I’m more optimistic than that. Higher education institutions are powerful. They’re powerful places from which ideas emit, and they have a pretty powerful and sometimes even transformative role in the lives of people.

If colleges were paying more attention to polarization, we could be doing a lot more to try to counter it, to reduce polarized attitudes among young people, perhaps even in ways that would spread out to affect their communities.

Colleges and universities have taken up many important social and other sorts of problems over the years. We haven’t recognized the extent to which polarization is just a serious ill.

Q: Your suggested solutions include increasing political diversity among students and faculty—an idea supported by many conservative critics of higher ed, but which some have condemned as “affirmative action for conservatives.” How do you suggest colleges and universities do this?

A: Ideologically diversifying the student body might include trying to identify people who are going to bring more positions on the right into higher ed, it could involve making sure that the student body includes plenty of center-right people, it could include making sure that the student body includes lots of Democratic Socialists.

The idea is that as admissions officers begin to think about what makes for an interesting class, it might be the case that they would find a way not by directly prioritizing ideology, but [by trying] to increase the ideological spread.

That could be through leaning into things that they’re already doing, like trying to recruit more students from rural areas. It could mean trying to recruit more students through venues that might have some association with different ideological positions—for example, networks tapped into religious institutions.

It’s much easier to have classes where students get into real, meaningful debates when there are really significant debates among students. It’s easier to tamp down cancel culture when there is real political diversity among the student body. I’m not suggesting that admissions officers admit students on the basis of their ideologies, but I do think that looking for ways to make sure that the student body has a kind of full spectrum of different positions is important.

On the faculty piece, I absolutely agree that affirmative action on the basis of ideology is not a good way to hire.

In the short term, one reasonable solution is to make faculty lines available in areas that would tend to attract a greater variety of applicants—these could be applicants on the right, it could be applicants more in the center—and then to allow existing departments to hire on the basis purely of academic merit.

Rural sociology has fallen out of fashion in many sociology departments. It’s not the case that everyone who studies rural sociology is on the center or on the right, but there’s evidence suggesting that they tend to be a little bit more right-leaning, certainly, than the average sociologist. So, if an academic administrator or president were to say, “Here’s a line in rural sociology, go hire the best person you see fit,” it would still be up to an academic department to find the person who meets the best academic qualifications.

Long term, I’m quite enthusiastic about efforts to encourage more young people with a whole variety of ideological views to consider higher education as a career. There are mentoring efforts that target undergraduates who are thinking about going to graduate school. There are efforts along those lines run right now through Johns Hopkins and AEI [American Enterprise Institute].

What we need to do to restore America’s confidence in higher education—and, in particular, restore the confidence of people on the right—has to be much broader than that, but I do think that is one part of the story.

Q: You reference multiple times—perhaps as an example of the negative impacts of polarization—the heated pro-Palestinian protests that occurred in the wake of the Oct. 7 [2023] attacks. But some faculty have criticized the push for more “civil discourse” at a time like this. Someone could argue that those protests were, on the whole, representative of something going right in higher ed: Students fervently demonstrating against ongoing bloodshed.

A: The main goal of the book was to understand the student experience and try to think through and understand the ways that polarization is affecting the lives of students—everything from how they choose schools, to whom they become friends with, what clubs they join, what they major in and, yes, also their participation in activism.

I bring up the pro-Palestine protests in the book primarily to make a larger point, which is that higher education is often a site of contestation, where people on the left have tried to use it to pursue their political ends, and people on the right.

Activism and protest is absolutely natural on college campuses. It’s part of civic learning, and something that we absolutely should not clamp down on or try to sway students from. I also think civil dialogue on college campuses is an important part of civil, civic learning and something we should be encouraging, and it’s when those two things become significantly in tension that problems arise.

Q: A lot of what you discuss here as both sources of problems and potential solutions seem to deal with issues that are only present at four-year institutions, especially selective ones.

A: I do focus in the book more on selective schools than on nonselective.

Some of the research in the book does cover the entire student population, excluding community colleges. But looking at four-year schools, these issues matter for students at a whole variety of institutions.

One of the questions that I asked … was “What have been the biggest sources of influence on your political views during your college years?” So focusing just on juniors and seniors, [who have] gone through more of the full arc of college, the No. 1 influence that they cited was their parents, which I think is fascinating. I think it speaks to a change in the nature of the college experience writ large, where parents remain in much closer contact with their kids.

High school students, for example, who have more conservative leanings may be sidestepping college altogether because of their concern that it’s too liberal of an environment for them, and that would keep them out of not just super-selective institutions, but potentially schools that would have more direct career relevance.

Students across the spectrum are concerned with political issues, worried about what’s happening in higher education, and want to see their way through to a good experience. And I think it’s incumbent upon those of us in higher education to make sure that we position them well to learn how to think critically, to acquire relevant career skills as part of the college experience but also to learn how to be more virtuous citizens who can be passionate in their views and active when necessary, but also not hate one another as they proceed along in their lives. And I think colleges have an important role to play there regardless of what kind they are.

title: Calif. Bill Could Create Designation for Asian-Serving Colleges
summary:
Calif. Bill Could Create Designation for Asian-Serving Colleges
Olivia.sanchez Wed, 08/19/2026 - 03:00 AM

The proposal doesn’t have a funding component but would require institutions to establish plans to better serve Asian American, Native Hawaiian and Pacific Islander students.

Byline(s)
Olivia Sanchez
full_text:
A bill moving through the California State Assembly would create a new designation for colleges in the state that serve large numbers of Asian American, Native Hawaiian or Pacific Islander (AANHPI) students. Although the bill itself doesn’t allocate any money to those institutions, advocates hope that they could eventually use the designation to access funding for initiatives that improve college access, retention and completion.

The proposed designation would mirror the federal Asian American and Native American Pacific Islander–serving institution designation, part of the Department of Education’s minority-serving institution program, which saw a $350 million cut last year. The federal designation, like the proposed state version, requires that colleges enroll a student body that is at least 11 percent AANHPI. California’s bill would also require colleges interested in earning the designation to submit a five-year plan outlining their academic-equity goals. They would need to explain how they’d address AANHPI outreach, academic and basic needs support, culturally responsive curriculum expansion, research initiatives, and improvement of transfer pathways, among other things.

The proposal is the latest in a string of efforts by state leaders to make up for federal programs that have been eliminated or defunded by the Trump administration. The California Legislature is considering a similar bill that would create a state Hispanic-serving institution designation for colleges that enroll a student body that is at least 25 percent Hispanic. Both the AANHPI and Hispanic-serving institution bills are modeled after the Black-serving institution designation California lawmakers established in 2024.

The bill, sponsored by Democratic Assembly Member Mike Fong, passed the Assembly 58 to 16. It will soon be up for a vote in the state Senate.

“California is home to one of the most diverse AANHPI student populations in the country, but too often, the unique disparities within our communities are overlooked. AB 2374 is about ensuring that colleges are intentionally serving students by investing in the resources and support they need to succeed,” Fong said in a statement. “With growing uncertainty around federal support for Minority-Serving Institutions, it is even more important that California establish its own framework to recognize institutions that demonstrate a meaningful commitment to AANHPI student success.”

Research shows AANHPI students are among the fastest-growing demographic groups in California, a trajectory that is projected to continue for the next several decades. Despite the population growth, AANHPI students still face significant challenges in higher education.

Alexis Takagi, a research analyst at the Campaign for College Opportunity, said that the model-minority myth—the belief that AANHPI students are uniformly high-achieving—masks major disparities among students from different ethnic groups.

For example, 61 percent of all Asian American adults in California have a bachelor’s degree, compared to 22 percent of Native Hawaiian and Pacific Islander adults and 30 percent of Cambodian, Hmong and Laotian adults, according to a recently released report from the Campaign for College Opportunity. Takagi, who co-authored the report, said the disparities are a result of several factors, including poverty, immigration status, English language proficiency and representation in higher education leadership.

“We really can’t treat AANHPI students as a monolith when there’s different needs, different barriers that students are experiencing across the educational pipeline,” Takagi said. “When we present data in the aggregate, it creates this false impression that they don’t really need support.”

Kirin A. Macapugay, a professor who serves as vice chair of the California Commission on Asian and Pacific Islander American Affairs, said that 17 of the state’s 84 institutions with at least 11 percent AANAPI students had been receiving funding through the federal program. She said the commission helped create this legislation as a way to encourage colleges to remain committed to serving this group of students.

“What we’re trying to ask these institutions is ‘Please, the services that you were able to provide with MSI funding, please don’t stop them. Please make sure that you continue serving our students and our communities,’” Macapugay said.

Through the federal MSI program, colleges could apply for grants for priorities such as laboratory upgrades, faculty professional development and student support services.

Rowena M. Tomaneng, deputy chancellor of the California Community College system, said she hopes this bill can create a pathway for future investment “when the economy gets better.” Until then, she thinks it could be a powerful tool for institutional accountability.

Tomaneng, who also serves as president of the board of Asian Pacific Americans in Higher Education, said the bill is meant to encourage institutions to provide students with the support they need to graduate, achieve greater socioeconomic mobility and contribute to the California economy.

title: Lawsuit Challenges New Length-of-Stay Limit for International Students
summary:
Lawsuit Challenges New Length-of-Stay Limit for International Students
Johanna Alonso Wed, 08/19/2026 - 03:00 AM

The rule, finalized last month, has drawn intense criticism from universities and international educators. Now, a group of eight organizations is arguing that it should be scrapped.

Byline(s)
Johanna Alonso
full_text:
Eight organizations representing the higher education and journalism sectors have sued the U.S. Department of Homeland Security over its rule limiting how long international students and journalists can stay in the country, which is slated to go into effect Sept. 15.

The lawsuit comes a month and a half after the highly controversial rule was finalized, altering a policy that had stood for nearly half a century that allowed international students to stay in the U.S. until they completed their program of study. Instead, students will be limited to four years unless they receive an extension. In the final rule, DHS said the cap is intended to prevent students from staying in the U.S. indefinitely, leading to overstays and national security concerns.

The complaint, filed Tuesday in the U.S. District Court for the District of Massachusetts, argued that DHS violated the Administrative Procedure Act, the statute that governs federal agencies, when it issued the final rule. The plaintiffs claim the department did not complete a thorough analysis of the potential impacts of the rule, failed to substantively respond to negative public comments and did not consider other possible solutions to address the concerns related to overstays, among other violations.

“DHS’s cost-benefit analysis is fundamentally defective,” the complaint reads. “The agency acknowledged billions of dollars in quantified costs over ten years, but listed zero quantitative benefits … And DHS also refused to quantify—and therefore largely disregarded altogether—the greatest harm of the Final Rule: the foreseeable decline in international student enrollment.”

NAFSA: Association of International Educators and the Presidents’ Alliance on Higher Education and Immigration, two organizations that have advocated against the rule since it was put forth last year, are among the plaintiffs on the case. Miriam Feldblum, president and CEO of the Presidents’ Alliance, said the central theme of the complaint is that DHS “did not engage in the reasoned decision-making that’s required by the APA.”

The rule drew massive scrutiny from the international education community. Higher education institutions argued that many students have legitimate reasons to study in the U.S. for more than four years and that extension requests would be burdensome both to institutions’ international student services offices and U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services, which will be responsible for evaluating the applications. The proposal received 22,000 public comments, the majority of which opposed the change.

In a statement to Inside Higher Ed, a DHS spokesperson wrote, “The performative outrage is incredible. Where was the outrage when foreign nationals were abusing the system, violating the terms of their student visas, and making a mockery of our immigration laws? If the media really cared about legitimate international students, they would be thanking President Trump for cracking down on the rampant fraud to ensure only those truly intending to study in the United States are given the privilege.”

The plaintiffs are asking the judge to vacate the rule and are seeking a preliminary injunction to prevent the rule from taking effect. In the motion requesting the injunction, the plaintiffs note that the rule is already affecting institutions and students, with colleges reporting that some international students have withdrawn their fall 2026 enrollment out of concern about the end of duration of status. Other institutions said that the number of applications they received from international students tanked this year.

“The detrimental harm of the rule impacts all institutional types, and the types of harms that are outlined in the declarations … [include] significant economic burdens on institutions,” said Feldblum. “As one of the institutions said, when students don’t come, that’s not a relationship that can be repaired. That is a loss for the institution.”

NAFSA has estimated that declines in international enrollment this academic year could cost the U.S. economy $3.4 billion.

title: Focus on the Quantum Future
summary:
Focus on the Quantum Future
jdimaggio@upcea.edu Wed, 08/19/2026 - 03:00 AM

We seem to be obsessed with artificial general intelligence and super intelligence. Yet, our forward focus today more appropriately should be on quantum computing.

Byline(s)
Ray Schroeder
full_text:
AI has had a remarkable impact on higher education since the release of GPT 3.5 in November 2022. For an inordinately long time, many faculty members fought access to the technology for students and imposed penalties for suspected use of AI in learning assessments. Not only were the initial “AI detector” attempts notoriously unsuccessful, this approach ignored the growing acceptance and reliance on AI in the workplace and resulting need for students to achieve AI literacy. Rather than denying access to AI in higher education, we should promote learning supported by AI among our students.

Attention has now shifted to the advancement of AI from generative to agentic models and the overall integration of AI into enterprise applications. These are important advancements in the field. Agentic approaches enable AI to take on roles within the organization that go beyond limited chatbots and rigidly defined operations to also perform self-assigned assessments, leading to new roles and activities to improve quality and efficiency. Further, recursive approaches enable algorithms to initiate self-improvement, ultimately proposing and independently implementing improvements.

While artificial general intelligence and artificial super intelligence will mark significant improvements in AI algorithms, there is not a single clear definition of either of these terms. Therefore, some experts believe that we have already achieved AGI and that ASI is just a year or two away; others say it will be the middle of the century before either is achieved. So, without minimizing the impact of any of the steps toward general and super intelligence, I think we are better served by focusing on more solidly defined steps in AI advancement.

Most Popular

That brings us to what may become a pivotal stage of development in AI, the use of stable quantum computing to accelerate and extend the potential of algorithms. This can begin with supercomputing digital computers linking to quantum computers to take advantage of the awesome speed and other capabilities of quantum physics. Many corporations already have constructed viable quantum computers. James Dargan reports in the Quantum Insider that there are at least 80 corporations that are heavily investing in the development of quantum computers: “IBM, Google, Microsoft and AWS are among the leading big tech players, each investing significantly in quantum R&D. IBM operates the world’s largest fleet of quantum systems through its Quantum Computation Center in New York, while Google achieved a landmark with its 105-qubit Willow chip.”

The National Institute of Standards and Technology earlier this year described some of the unique characteristics of quantum computers:

One of the “strange, often counterintuitive laws” referenced above that govern subatomic physics is the phenomenon of superposition. That is, the ability of incredibly tiny particles to hold multiple, seemingly exclusive, properties at the same time. Much as digital computers use bits, quantum computers use qubits. The superposition of a qubit allows it to exist in a combination of both the 0 and 1 states simultaneously. For at least a brief period of time needed to complete computations, qubits can be counted as 0, 1 or a simultaneous combination of 0 and 1 at that given time. This results in an exponential acceleration in the capability of quantum computers to do their work compared to digital computers.

Another quality of qubits is that they can become entangled and share properties such as polarity. This entanglement enables them to be separated, potentially by tens of thousands of miles, and retain a special affinity to their entangled partner. For example, if one changes the polarity of one qubit, the entangled partner qubit changes polarity instantly, at the very same instant, not just at the speed of light. In the case of entangled qubits distanced thousands of miles away from each other, monitored with atomic clocks, the change weirdly takes place at the very same instant.

Arguably, the most famous theoretical physicist of all time found this action extraordinary:

A combination of these quantum characteristics and qualities has essentially enabled subatomic teleportation over tiny distances. These are all characteristics of subatomic quantum physics rather than the Newtonian physics that we are familiar with in everyday life.

The application of these features to AI algorithms greatly expands and accelerates their speed. Initially, this is experimentally being accomplished by linking supercomputers to quantum computers and even creating hybrid computers. One of the more concerning aspects of the incredible speed and power of quantum processing is its impact on cyberencryption, which is used for privacy in many applications worldwide.

The overwhelming speed of quantum enables quantum computers to break encryptions. In the very near future, it is anticipated that all online encryption will be vulnerable to hacking using public keys attacked by quantum computing. Imagine all privacy—at universities, banks, departments of defense and beyond—becoming vulnerable on the same day when a computer reaches the speed and complexity to crack all codes.

In Forbes, Chuck Brooks warns,

A dramatic reminder of the impending importance of Q-day can be found at the Q-Day Countdown site. At the time of writing of this column, the site is displaying Google’s estimation of the time to the date of Q-day showing 876 days, 7 hours, 59 minutes and 12 seconds. That would be Jan. 1, 2030. Check out the site yourself if you would like a reminder of when our financial systems may collapse if we fail to provide some sort of prior intervention.

I remain hopeful that some ingenious new mode of encryption (mind meld?) may be discovered to avoid the catastrophe. I am only beginning to imagine ways in which the unique features of quantum computing may enhance distance teaching and learning. In the meantime, we should remain aware that AI will continue to improve, but a massive quantum leap is most likely to be seen when we engage quantum computers in advancing AI, especially in the next two or three years. Is your institution prepared for the broad ramifications of quantum computing? Do you have an operable quantum computer on campus for teaching and research purposes? Who is leading your institution in quantum thought and action?

title: NCERT recasts political science textbook panel; 4 with RSS links among 20 members
summary: NCERT has recast the team for preparing political science textbooks for Classes XI and XII, with one of the two books slated to be ready by Nov. The 20-member panel includes faculty from JNU, DU, IGNOU and NLU Delhi, among others. At least four members have links, past or present, with organisations associated with RSS-BJP.
full_text:
The 20-member panel includes faculty members from JNU, Delhi University, Ignou, National Law University Delhi, Jindal Global Law School, Pondicherry University and Utkal University.

NEW DELHI: NCERT has reconstituted the team tasked with preparing political science textbooks for Classes XI and XII, bringing together university academics, schoolteachers and its own faculty members, with the first of the two books scheduled to be ready by Nov. The 20-member panel includes faculty members from JNU, Delhi University, Ignou, National Law University Delhi, Jindal Global Law School, Pondicherry University and Utkal University, schoolteachers and NCERT academics, with at least four of its members known for links, past or present, with organisations linked to RSS or BJP. They are former ABVP national secretary and JNU professor Vandana Mishra; educationist Yadunath Deshpande, who has held organisational positions in ABVP and has described himself professionally as a BJP political consultant; Prashant Divekar of Pune-based Jnana Prabodhini; and JNU academic Ravi Rameshchandra Shukla, who has been associated with the editorial board of a journal published by Rambhau Mhalgi Prabodhini-linked Indian Institute of Democratic Leadership. The composition of the panel, however, is considerably broader, with it also having Prakash Kandpal and Ravi Shukla from JNU, Needhi Gupta from NLU Delhi, Chetan Singhai from Chanakya University, Sukanshika Vatsa from Delhi University and Satish Kumar from Ignou, among others.

The Textbook Development Team (TDT), headed by political analyst and academic Sandeep Shastri, vice-president of Nitte (Deemed to be University), has been asked to finalise the Class XI textbook by Nov 30, 2026, and the Class XII book by July 30, 2027. NCERT said the reconstitution of the team was intended to "further strengthen and streamline" preparation of the two textbooks. title: RSS-linked academics in NCERT textbook panel
summary: The textbook team will be led by academic and political analyst Sandeep Shastri, vice-president of Karnataka-based deemed university Nitte.
full_text:
The NCERT has reconstituted the textbook development team for classes 11 and 12 political science with a mandate to integrate cultural rootedness, Indian knowledge systems and inclusion, with at least four of the members having direct or indirect links with the RSS.

The team has been asked to develop the class 11 textbook by November and the class 12 book by July next year.

The textbook team will be led by academic and political analyst Sandeep Shastri, vice-president of Karnataka-based deemed university Nitte.

Among the members of the textbook development team are at least four academics and educationists with direct or indirect documented backgrounds in the RSS-affiliated Akhil Bharatiya Vidyarthi Parishad (ABVP) and the BJP.

Yadunath Deshpande, now a senior consultant with the Ministry of Education, has a longstanding organisational background in the ABVP. The organisation's own records identify him as its joint state organising secretary for Maharashtra in the past. He subsequently served as an organising secretary in the ABVP's Mumbai-Konkan structure. His LinkedIn profile also describes him as a political consultant for the BJP.

Prashant Divekar has a longstanding association with Pune-based Jnana Prabodhini, an RSS-affiliated institution. It was founded in 1962 by Vinayak Vishwanath, an RSS member and pracharak. In his profile on the National Council for Teacher Education’s National Mission for Mentoring portal, Mr. Divekar describes his approach as being “rooted in Bhartiya educational philosophy” and says he has contributed to the National Curriculum Framework.” Vandana Mishra, professor at JNU’s Centre for Political Studies, is a former national secretary of the ABVP.

In 2021, Devendra Fadnavis had become its president. Prof. Shukla has also undertaken research centred on cultural and spiritual nationalism. He is the principal investigator of an ICSSR-funded JNU project titled "The Role of Fests in Shaping of Spiritual and Cultural Nationalism of Bharat: A Study of Kumbha and Magh Mela".

The team also comprises Prakash Kandpal from JNU, Needhi Gupta from National Law University, Chetan Singhai from Chanakya University, Sukanshika Vatsa from Delhi University, Satish Kumar from IGNOU, Deevanshu Shrivastava from National University of Study and Research in Law, Pranav Gupta from Jindal Global Law School, Nanda Kishor from Pondicherry University and Swapna Prabhu from Utkal University.
